title: Weather, nature & seasons
goal: Talk about the weather and the seasons, describe the landscape, and say what's going to happen (it's going to rain).
intro:
Maharashtra has three seasons: **उन्हाळा** (hot summer, March–May), **पावसाळा** (the monsoon, June–September — the season everyone talks about) and **हिवाळा** (mild winter). Marathi weather talk is full of verbs: rain 'falls' (पाऊस पडतो), sunshine 'falls' too (ऊन पडलं), wind 'is let loose' (वारा सुटला), and cold 'rings' in your body (थंडी वाजते).

You'll also learn the very useful **-णार** form for 'going to': पाऊस पडणार आहे 'it's going to rain'.

phrases.en: Take an umbrella, it's going to rain.
In the monsoon everything is green.
What will the weather be like tomorrow?

grammar.title: Weather expressions
grammar.body:
English uses a dummy 'it' (it's raining). Marathi names the weather itself as the subject, with a suitable verb:

**पाऊस पडतो / पडतोय** 'rain falls / is falling' (पाऊस m)
**ऊन पडलं आहे** / **ऊन आहे** 'it's sunny'
**वारा सुटला आहे** 'it's windy (the wind has got up)'
**ढग आले आहेत** 'clouds have come'
**थंडी पडली आहे** 'the cold has set in'

Some are truly impersonal neuter verbs: **उकडतंय** 'it's sweltering', **अंधार पडतोय** 'it's getting dark'.

How it feels to **you** uses the dative: मला थंडी वाजतेय 'I feel cold', मला उकडतंय 'I'm hot'.

examples.en: There's a strong wind at the sea.
It's getting dark, let's go home.

grammar.title: 'Going to': the -णार form
grammar.body:
Stem + **णार** + आहे expresses something that is **going to** happen or is **planned**: पाऊस पडणार आहे 'it's going to rain', मी जाणार आहे 'I'm going to go'.

-णार itself doesn't change for gender or person; the आहे after it does: मी येणार आहे, तू येणार आहेस, ते येणार आहेत. In speech आहे is often dropped: उद्या पाऊस पडणार 'it'll rain tomorrow', तू येणार? 'are you coming?'

**Negative:** -णार नाही: आज पाऊस पडणार नाही 'it won't rain today'.

(Unit 17 covers the simple future tense as well.)

examples.en: It's going to rain this evening.
The cold is going to increase next week.
We're going to go to the beach.

dialogue.title: A monsoon trek
dialogue.setting: Riya wants to drag her friend Om on a rainy-season trek to Sinhagad fort near Pune.

lines.speaker: Riya
lines.en: Shall we go to Sinhagad this Sunday?

lines.speaker: Om
lines.en: In the rain? Have you seen the forecast?

lines.speaker: Riya
lines.native: हो, हलका पाऊस पडणार आहे. पण सकाळी ऊन असेल.
lines.roman: ho, halkā pāūs paḍṇār āhe. paṇ sakāḷī ūn asel.
lines.en: Yes, there'll be light rain. But it'll be sunny in the morning.

lines.speaker: Om
lines.native: डोंगरावर खूप धुकं असतं, आणि वारा पण.
lines.roman: ḍoṅgarāvar khūp dhukaṃ astaṃ, āṇi vārā paṇ.
lines.en: There's always a lot of fog on the hill, and wind too.

lines.speaker: Riya
lines.native: तीच तर मजा आहे! ढग, धुकं, धबधबे...
lines.roman: tīts tar madzā āhe! ḍhag, dhukaṃ, dhabdhabe...
lines.en: That's exactly the fun! Clouds, mist, waterfalls...

lines.speaker: Om
lines.native: ठीक आहे. पण छत्री आणि जॅकेट घे.
lines.roman: ṭhīk āhe. paṇ chhatrī āṇi jækeṭ ghe.
lines.en: OK. But bring an umbrella and a jacket.

lines.speaker: Riya
lines.en: What's the use of an umbrella? We're going to get soaked anyway!

lines.speaker: Om
lines.native: खरं आहे. मग सकाळी सहाला निघूया.
lines.roman: kharaṃ āhe. mag sakāḷī sahālā nighūyā.
lines.en: True. Then let's leave at six in the morning.

culture: The monsoon is Maharashtra's favourite season. When the first rains arrive in June, people celebrate with hot **कांदाभजी** (onion fritters) and चहा, and weekend treks to the Sahyadri forts — Sinhagad, Rajgad, Lohagad, built or captured by Shivaji Maharaj — are a Pune and Mumbai ritual. The monsoon is also when Mumbai floods, trains stop, and offices give everyone a 'rainy day'.
